human_code: the instruction sheet itself, compiled: every character of CLAUDE.md mapped to the sentence that causes it

nodes.text:
the instruction sheet turns claude into the compiler.

human code arrives in prose.
the compiler emits the sentences, the code, the map, and the registry.
the map connects every sentence to the characters it caused.

one folder holds a program.

each file's name is a short word that describes the node plus a 3 digit combination
child appear only when lowering adds real meaning.
build/ holds the "compiled" code file, its map, and the concept registry file.

projects.json then registers the project's name and human code.

the folder tree is only the authoring tree.
it records which sentence refines which, nothing else.

causation lives exclusively in the map.
the map is keyed by each sentence's stable 4-hex @id.

the two relations may disagree.
that disagreement is information, not an error.

the map is one json file.
it holds program, human_code, code_file, the node list, and the fragments.

each fragment carries an owner-set of node ids over character ranges.
several ids mean joint causation.

an empty owner-set on an assumed fragment means pure convention.
a why then stands in for user prose.

any two ranges must nest or be disjoint.
a contribution that would straddle another fragment's range is emitted as several split ranges instead.

containment is then a valid poset.
the deepest cover of a character is therefore well defined.

a node's range is completely tiled by deeper fragments.
code no child sentence causes is attributed to the sentence that forces it, or owned up to in an assumed fragment with a why.

a gap is a compile error.
coverage is verified by computation before the map is emitted.

the tightest container ranges a node's code hangs under must form an antichain.
a node straddling a parent and that parent's ancestor is split at its true depth, or the missing parent sentence is written.

levels are never declared.
they fall out of containment.

reword - the words change, the meaning does not.
update the .human file and the map text. touch nothing else.

revise - the meaning changes.
a revise reads the registry first.
rewrite only the code that the change forces. keep all untouched code byte for byte. move only the ranges that moved.
a changed concept recompiles every node that points to it.

offsets index the LF-normalized code string exactly.
offsets are computed, never guessed.
range edges snap to token or line boundaries.

the assert: lines are the only ground truth.
never ship a map describing code that fails its asserts.

the web app only renders what the compiler emits.
it decides nothing.

the v1 rules carry forward at the close of the sheet.
what bound the compiler before still binds.
one list gathers them.

a specified fragment traces to the user's words.
an assumed fragment fills a gap by convention.

a note: line in a .human file is for the human only.
it is never compiled.
it never causes any range.

the compiler keeps a concept registry.
each concept gets one id.
each node points to the ids of its concepts.

the registry file is readable and diffable.

when a concept changes, every node that points to it recompiles.

the LLM reads one node and lists its concepts.
each concept carries a name, a type, and a signature.
the list is rebuilt only when the node changes.

the compiler then finds candidate pairs without the LLM.
near names, near embeddings, or equal signatures make a pair.
pairs with different types are removed.

the LLM examines one candidate pair at a time.

do not ask if the two concepts are the same.
the LLM says yes too often.

ask for one example where the two concepts cause different results.
an example means different.
no example means same.

the compiler writes the decision and the example in the registry.

the match is tested by ablation.
change the concept, recompile, and the code of each connected node must change.
a match that moves no code goes back to examination.

matches are never chained.
a matching b and b matching c does not make a match c.
each new concept is compared with all members of the group.
